6.7. Finite-Time Behavior🔗

The linear existence theorems work on prescribed finite time intervals. For nonlinear parabolic equations, the length of that interval can itself become a question: a reaction term can outrun diffusion and force a norm to infinity in finite time, and Keller–Segel aggregation can concentrate mass. The finite-time results include the large-data obstruction for nonlinear heat and moment-based obstructions for Keller–Segel.

6.7.1. Finite-Time Growth, Lifespan, and Similarity🔗

6.7.1.1. Solutions, Growth, and Continuation🔗

A formula that grows quickly is only a candidate. A finite-time singularity statement exhibits a solution on times before some finite horizon and proves that a specified norm or observable becomes unbounded as that horizon approaches. We formalize the pieces separately: the solution concept, the maximal-time or norm-divergence predicate, the mechanism forcing the growth, and its application to the original PDE.

With the pieces kept apart, different arguments can be compared. Explicit solutions, Riccati comparison, weighted moments, virial identities, and self-similar profiles all appear, and each proves a different kind of conclusion.

6.7.1.2. Reusable Growth Mechanisms🔗

A Banach-space trajectory blows up when its norm tends to infinity from the left of a finite time. The associated theorems transfer blow-up through scalar amplitudes, linear isometries, and bounded remainders, and prove that such a trajectory cannot have a continuous extension across the singular time.

For spatial fields, the corresponding supremum-norm predicate can be proved from one diverging sample or from a weighted moment.

The Riccati model y'=cy^2, with c>0 and a positive initial value, gives the basic differential-inequality mechanism. Its explicit solution diverges at an explicit horizon. A trajectory with the same initial value satisfying y'\ge cy^2 up to that horizon blows up there; if the inequality holds on a closed interval, the interval ends strictly before the horizon.

6.7.1.3. Equation-Specific Branches🔗

The nonlinear heat branch begins on a bounded domain, where a first Dirichlet eigenfunction moment excludes nonnegative weak solutions with large initial data on a prescribed interval. On the whole space it contains a complete example: a nonnegative spatially constant classical solution is verified directly and its spatial supremum norm is proved to blow up at finite time. The same chapter derives Type I and scaling-invariant profile equations. These profile theorems say when an ansatz solves the PDE and when its scale forces concentration; the profile itself is a hypothesis.

The parabolic Keller–Segel branch derives the density and potential profile equations under the standard similarity scaling. A pair of C^2 profiles satisfying both equations, with nonnegative density profile, generates a classical pre-singular solution. A bounded density profile with one nonzero value makes the density ansatz blow up in the spatial supremum norm.

The virial branch follows a different route. An affine second-moment identity and nonnegativity constrain the right endpoint of a solution interval by an explicit horizon. This is a lifespan theorem: it rules out continuation of a solution retaining the stated moment properties beyond that time.

The abnormal three-dimensional scaling is analyzed as an obstruction calculation. Its amplitude diverges and its diffusion coefficient vanishes in rescaled variables, but the physical residual can diverge. Under the aggregation profile equation, the exact criterion says that the density residual vanishes everywhere precisely when the density profile is harmonic.

6.7.1.4. Types of Conclusion🔗

Four kinds of conclusion serve different purposes:

  • a residual identity computes the error of an ansatz;

  • a profile equivalence says the residual vanishes exactly when the reduced equations hold;

  • a solution theorem proves the original PDE on the pre-singular domain;

  • a blow-up or lifespan theorem proves norm divergence or a finite endpoint.

A singularity result must connect an actual solution to norm divergence or a proved obstruction to continuation. For an ansatz, a sufficient profile condition and its analytic hypotheses can establish the solution; a converse profile equivalence is useful but not required. The explicit nonlinear-heat theorem is both a solution theorem and a blow-up theorem; the virial and Riccati theorems are lifespan theorems for intervals carrying their stated hypotheses.

6.7.1.5. Finite-Time Singularity Interfaces🔗

6.7.1.5.1. Mathematical Context🔗

Finite-time blow-up can prevent a nonlinear parabolic solution from existing globally. Starting from smooth initial data, we ask whether a solution remains smooth or a specified norm becomes unbounded as t approaches a finite time T.

The mechanisms studied here are equation-independent: they reduce the PDE question to an ODE comparison. The prototypical argument has three steps:

  1. Derive a differential inequality. A suitable functional of the solution (a weighted moment, an eigenfunction projection, or a spatial norm) satisfies y'\geq ay^p for some p>1.

  2. Compare with the ODE. Assume a>0 and y_0>0. The inequality y'\geq ay^2 (the Riccati case p=2) is compared with the exact ODE solution y(t)=y_0/(1-ay_0(t-t_0)), which blows up at the horizon T=t_0+1/(ay_0).

  3. Transfer to the PDE. The comparison bounds the time interval on which the functional can remain finite. An estimate relating the functional to a PDE norm transfers this obstruction to the solution; a continuation theorem is needed to identify the endpoint of its maximal lifespan.

This strategy appears in Kaplan (1963) for eigenfunction moments, Fujita (1966) for critical exponents, Levine (1973) for concavity methods, and Evans (2010, pp. 547–549) for the weighted eigenfunction argument. To apply the proved comparison and transfer results, a model must supply its differential inequality, the required positivity and interval regularity, and the estimate connecting its observable to the chosen PDE norm.

A trajectory u : \mathbb R\to E in a type equipped with a norm blows up at T when

\lVert u(t)\rVert\longrightarrow+\infty\qquad\text{as }t\uparrow T.

This is an equation-independent predicate. It can be applied to scalar observables, Banach-space solution trajectories, and Sobolev- or L^p-valued evolutions.

    def PDE.Solution.Singularity.FiniteTime.NormBlowsUpAt.{u_1}
  {E : Type u_1} [Norm E] (u : ℝ → E)
  (T : ℝ) : Prop

    A trajectory blows up in norm at T from below if its norm tends to +∞ along t < T.

Because the predicate concerns only the scalar function t\mapsto\lVert u(t)\rVert, blow-up can be transported by any operation whose effect on norms is controlled. Multiplication by a scalar amplitude, composition with a linear isometry, and addition of an eventually bounded error are three such operations; the amplitude case is the one that similarity profiles use.

Let E be a seminormed module over a normed field \mathbb K. If \lVert A(t)\rVert\to+\infty as t\uparrow T and a profile family v(t)\in E satisfies

c\le \lVert v(t)\rVert

eventually for some c>0, then A(t)v(t) blows up in the norm of E. This is the quotient-friendly route for Sobolev and L^p profiles: once a dilation or pullback has been defined on the function space itself, the argument needs only a lower norm bound and never chooses a pointwise representative.

    A diverging scalar amplitude forces norm blow-up when the profile trajectory stays uniformly away from zero in norm.

    The scalar field and state space are arbitrary normed modules. In particular, profile t may belong to a Sobolev or Lᵖ quotient space; any dilation used to define that trajectory has to be constructed separately.

Proof for Theorem 6.137
uses 0

By the scalar-multiplication norm identity, the norm of the product is \lVert A(t)\rVert\lVert v(t)\rVert. Eventually this is bounded below by c\lVert A(t)\rVert. Multiplication by the positive constant c preserves convergence to +\infty, so the product norm also diverges.

The amplitude theorem runs in one direction only: a divergent amplitude produces blow-up. A linear isometry preserves the norm exactly, so with it the transfer is an equivalence.

    A linear isometric embedding preserves and reflects norm blow-up of an abstract trajectory.

    The source and target may themselves be Sobolev or Lᵖ spaces. The statement uses only their norms and the isometry; it does not select pointwise representatives.

Proof for Theorem 6.138
uses 0

Unfold norm blow-up and composition. A linear isometry satisfies \lVert Lu\rVert=\lVert u\rVert pointwise, so the two convergence statements are identical.

An isometry changes the trajectory without changing its norm. A singular leading term plus a controlled correction changes the norm by an eventually bounded amount.

If \lVert u(t)-v(t)\rVert is eventually bounded as t\uparrow T, then u blows up at T if and only if v does. Thus an eventually bounded remainder neither creates nor removes norm blow-up.

    Norm blow-up is invariant under an eventually norm-bounded additive error.

    Thus a singular leading trajectory and its uniformly controlled perturbation blow up together. The bounded-difference hypothesis is symmetric because ‖u - v‖ = ‖v - u‖.

Proof for Theorem 6.139
uses 0

Suppose \lVert u-v\rVert\leq C eventually. To force \lVert v(t)\rVert above a threshold R, first force \lVert u(t)\rVert above R+C. The triangle inequality \lVert u\rVert\leq\lVert u-v\rVert+\lVert v\rVert then gives the desired bound. The reverse implication is the same argument after using \lVert v-u\rVert=\lVert u-v\rVert.

A trajectory whose norm blows up at T has no left-continuous extension through T. More precisely, there is no function continuous within (-\infty,T] at T that agrees with the trajectory for every t<T.

    Norm blow-up rules out a trajectory continuous from the left through T that agrees with the original trajectory at every earlier time.

    Such an extension would give the original trajectory a finite left limit at T, contradicting norm divergence.

Proof for Theorem 6.140
uses 0

A continuous extension v would converge to the finite value v(T) from within (-\infty,T]. Restrict this convergence to times below T and use the pointwise agreement v=u there. This gives a finite left limit for u, contradicting norm blow-up.

That obstruction uses the norm alone. Paired with an existence statement for integral curves it becomes a continuation alternative: for an autonomous C^1 field on a complete space, an integral curve that fails to continue past a finite time can have no limit there, and norm blow-up is one way for the limit to fail.

Theorem6.141
Group: Finite-time blow-up models (57)

Definition 6.136
Loading preview

uses 1used by 0✓L∃∀N

Let E be a complete real normed space, f:E\to E, a<b, and let u:\mathbb R\to E be an integral curve of the autonomous equation

u'(t)=f(u(t))\qquad(a<t<b).

If u(t)\to x as t\uparrow b and f is C^1 at x, then there are c>b and v:\mathbb R\to E with v=u on (a,b) and v'(t)=f(v(t)) for all t\in(a,c). The same conclusion holds when u is Cauchy as t\uparrow b and f is C^1 at every point, and, without completeness, when a local solution through (b,x) on some (b-\varepsilon,b+\varepsilon) is supplied and f is merely continuous at x.

Conversely, in any normed group, if \lVert u(t)\rVert\to+\infty as t\uparrow T, then no v:\mathbb R\to E with v(t)=u(t) for all t<T is continuous within (-\infty,T] at T. The same holds along any nontrivial clock \sigma\to T^- for which \lVert u(\sigma(s))\rVert\to+\infty, and more basically a trajectory whose norm tends to infinity along a nontrivial filter converges to no point.

The obstruction half is the no-extension theorem for norm blow-up stated without the blow-up predicate, together with its reparametrized and raw-filter variants.

    A trajectory whose norm tends to infinity cannot converge to a point of its normed state space.

Proof for Theorem 6.141
uses 0

For continuation, extend u to \bar u by the value x at b. On (a,b) the derivative f(u(t)) tends to f(x), so \bar u has left derivative f(x) at b. Since f is C^1 at x, the Picard–Lindelöf theorem supplies a local solution w with w(b)=x on (b-\varepsilon,b+\varepsilon). Define v=\bar u for t\le b and v=w for t\ge b. Away from b the curve v locally coincides with a solution; at b its left and right derivatives are both f(x), so v is differentiable there with the correct derivative. In the Cauchy form, completeness produces the limit x.

For the obstruction, a left-continuous extension v would give u(t)=v(t)\to v(T) as t\uparrow T, hence \lVert u(t)\rVert\to\lVert v(T)\rVert<\infty, contradicting divergence of the norm.

Everything so far concerns a single trajectory in a normed space. A spatial field u(x,t) has no preferred norm; the pointwise supremum over x is the least committal choice, and since a slice may be unbounded the supremum has to be allowed the value +\infty.

✓L∃∀N

For a field u : X\to\mathbb R\to E, the pointwise spatial supremum is the extended nonnegative real

S_u(t)=\sup_{x\in X}\operatorname{ofReal}\lVert u(x,t)\rVert \in\mathbb R_{\ge0}\cup\{+\infty\}.

In Lean this is ⨆ x, ENNReal.ofReal ‖u x t‖. An unbounded spatial slice therefore has value +\infty. The limit S_u(t)\to+\infty alone does not identify a blow-up time: the stationary field u(x,t)=x on \mathbb R has S_u(t)=+\infty at every time.

SpatialSupNormBlowsUpAt u T requires both this limit as t\uparrow T and finite spatial slices for all t<T sufficiently close to T. The finite bound may depend on t; no uniform bound in time is imposed. General divergence statements use Tendsto (spatialSupNorm u) directly, so they also apply to fields with unbounded slices.

This is a pointwise supremum: changing one value of u can change S_u. Sobolev and L^p trajectories use norm divergence at the finite horizon in their own normed state space, for example through the scalar-amplitude blow-up criterion.

    Finiteness is required only near T, with no uniform bound in time. In particular, a field whose spatial slices are already unbounded throughout a left neighborhood of T does not blow up in this sense. No PDE solution predicate is part of the definition: equation modules establish the equation and blow-up separately.

A supremum dominates each of its terms, so divergence of the field along one spatial sample, which may move with time, already forces divergence of S_u.

Proof for Theorem 6.143
uses 0

For every time t, the sampled quantity \operatorname{ofReal}\lVert u(x(t),t)\rVert is one term in the supremum defining S_u(t). The sampled norm tends to +\infty, hence so does its ENNReal.ofReal image. Monotonicity of convergence to the top element then transfers the limit to S_u. Together with the supplied finite-slice condition, this proves divergence of the spatial supremum norm.

For a similarity ansatz the natural sample is the physical point x(t)=x_0+(T-t)^{\beta}y_0, whose similarity coordinate stays at y_0; along it the profile value is frozen and only the amplitude (T-t)^{-\alpha} varies. Every ansatz divergence theorem in the equation-specific chapters works this way. A positive amplitude exponent and one nonzero profile value suffice for divergence. A bounded profile also gives finite spatial slices, so the field satisfies the blow-up predicate.

✓L∃∀N

A pointwise profile f : X \to E, amplitude exponent \alpha, spatial exponent \beta, center x_0, and time T determine

u(x,t)=(T-t)^{-\alpha} f\!\left((T-t)^{-\beta}(x-x_0)\right).

The pointwise construction is polymorphic in the spatial and value types: scalar, vector-valued, complex-valued, and system profiles can share it when the required real scaling operations exist. This is a pointwise profile construction; it assumes no differentiability until an equation-specific theorem requires it.

An L^p or Sobolev profile is instead an almost-everywhere equivalence class. Its similarity theory needs dilation pullbacks on that quotient and a weak form of the reduced equation, instead of pointwise composition. Once the quotient-level pullback is available, the scalar-amplitude blow-up criterion supplies the abstract amplitude-times-profile step.

✓L∃∀N

For a scalar field u, measure \mu, and spatial weight w, define

\mathcal M_w[u](t)=\int_X w(x)u(x,t)\,d\mu(x).

The spatial type and measure are arbitrary. Euclidean geometry enters only through a model-specific choice of weight. Mathlib's Bochner integral is totalized, so the weighted spatial moment is defined even for a nonintegrable integrand, where the integral is set to zero. Every theorem that reads this expression as a moment therefore assumes integrability.

Proof for Theorem 6.146
uses 0

First bound the absolute value of the Bochner integral by the integral of the absolute value and rewrite that integral as a nonnegative extended integral. Almost everywhere, nonnegativity of w and the definition of S_u(t) give |w(x)u(x,t)|\leq w(x)S_u(t). Monotonicity of the nonnegative Lebesgue integral permits this pointwise bound, after which the constant S_u(t) is pulled outside. Integrability and nonnegativity of w identify the remaining extended integral with \operatorname{ofReal}\int_X w\,d\mu.

Dividing the estimate by a positive mass turns it into a lower bound for S_u(t) in terms of the moment, so once a PDE argument has driven |\mathcal M_w[u](t)| to infinity the supremum must follow.

For y'=a y^2 with initial value y(t_0)=y_0, the explicit candidate is

y(t)=\frac{y_0}{1-a y_0(t-t_0)}, \qquad T=t_0+\frac{1}{a y_0}.

The formula is total as a Lean function, including at its pole. Analytic statements therefore work on t<T under a y_0>0.

Evans notes the scalar model y'=y^2 before beginning the weighted eigenfunction argument. The theorem carries a coefficient a, an arbitrary initial time, and the horizon formula.

    The distinguished horizon t₀ + (a * y₀)⁻¹ of the explicit Riccati formula.

    When a * y₀ ≠ 0, this is the unique zero of the denominator. It is a future pole only when a * y₀ > 0. If a * y₀ = 0, then 1 / 0 = 0 makes the horizon equal to t₀, and there is no pole.

The formula is only a candidate until its derivative has been computed. The relevant hypothesis is the sign of the product a y_0, not separate signs of a and y_0.

6.7.1.5.5. Quadratic differential-growth comparison🔗

The Riccati solution y(t)=1/(a(T-t)) is the comparison function for blow-up arguments. A trajectory satisfying y'\geq ay^2 is compared with it by differentiating 1/y, bounding its derivative by -a, and integrating.

This comparison principle is a standard engine behind ODE-based blow-up results for parabolic equations. The mathematical content varies from problem to problem: Kaplan uses a first-eigenfunction moment, Fujita uses scaling, and Levine uses a concavity inequality. The Riccati comparison is one scalar tool for turning differential growth into a finite-time obstruction. Evans (2010, pp. 548–549) uses it to conclude the blow-up theorem for superlinear heat equations.

Let y(t_0)>0 and a\ge0. If y is continuous on [t_0,T], differentiable in its interior, and

a\,y(t)^2\le y'(t),

then positivity propagates and

\frac{1}{y(t)} \le \frac{1}{y(t_0)}-a(t-t_0).

No separate positivity hypothesis is needed away from t_0: monotonicity supplies it.

Evans obtains the related inequality \eta'\ge -\lambda_1\eta+\eta^2 for a weighted PDE observable and removes the linear term by an exponential change of variables. The Lean theorem is the autonomous quadratic comparison step of that argument.

Proof for Theorem 6.152
uses 0

The differential inequality first shows that y is nondecreasing, hence it stays positive after t_0. The reciprocal is therefore differentiable in the interior, with \left(\frac1y\right)'=-\frac{y'}{y^2}\leq-a. Apply the mean-value inequality to 1/y on [t_0,t] and rearrange the result.

The reciprocal bound is stated on a closed interval [t_0,T], but it already contains the blow-up: its right-hand side equals a(\tau-t) for \tau=t_0+1/(a y(t_0)), so y(t)\ge 1/(a(\tau-t)) before the horizon.

Proof for Theorem 6.153
uses 0

For each t before the horizon \tau, restrict the hypotheses to the compact interval [t_0,t] and apply the reciprocal estimate. Its right-hand side is exactly a(\tau-t), and positivity permits inversion, giving (a(\tau-t))^{-1}\leq y(t). The lower bound tends to +\infty as t\uparrow\tau, so order comparison proves divergence of y and hence norm blow-up.

If the hypotheses are instead known on a closed interval [t_0,T], the same estimate says something about T rather than about a limit: the horizon cannot belong to the interval, because there the right-hand side would be zero while 1/y>0. This endpoint form bounds whatever interval the hypotheses hold on; T need not be a maximal time.

6.7.1.6. Nonlinear Heat Singularity Profiles🔗

6.7.1.6.1. Large data on a bounded domain🔗

On a bounded domain with zero Dirichlet boundary data, a nonzero spatial constant is unavailable. A positive first eigenfunction instead measures the part of the solution on which reaction can overcome diffusion. The theorem constructs this weight from the domain and derives its moment inequality from the weak PDE.

Let \Omega\subset\mathbb R^n, n>0, be nonempty, bounded, connected, and open, and let a<b. The domain admits a positive first Dirichlet eigenweight w\in H^1_0(\Omega) with eigenvalue \lambda>0 and \int_\Omega w=1. Suppose F, not necessarily differentiable, is convex on the nonnegative half-line, with

F(s)\ge c s^p\quad(s\ge0),\qquad c>0,\quad p>1.

For initial datum u_a\in L^2(\Omega), set M_0=\int_\Omega w u_a. If M_0>0 and

M_0^{1-p}\le (p-1)c\,e^{-\lambda(b-a)(p-1)}(b-a),

there is no nonnegative weak energy solution of u_t-\Delta u=F(u) on [a,b] with zero Dirichlet boundary data and initial datum u_a.

Precisely, the excluded class has u\in L^2((a,b);H^1_0(\Omega)) and a dual forcing \ell\in L^2((a,b);H^{-1}(\Omega)) satisfying the integrated weak heat equation with that initial trace. For almost every time, u\ge0 almost everywhere in space, and for every v\in H^1_0(\Omega), vF(u) is integrable and \ell(v)=\int_\Omega vF(u). The threshold is a sufficient condition for nonexistence on the prescribed interval [a,b].

Proof for Theorem 6.155
uses 0

The first Dirichlet eigenfunction gives a positive probability weight. Lions–Magenes regularity supplies the continuous L^2 representative of the weak solution, and pairing its integrated derivative with w gives an absolutely continuous moment M(t)=\int_\Omega w u(t), with M(a)=M_0. The weak eigen-equation identifies diffusion as \lambda M. The reaction identity and weighted Jensen inequality then give, almost everywhere,

M'(t)+\lambda M(t)=\int_\Omega wF(u(t)) \ge F(M(t))\ge c M(t)^p.

For z(t)=e^{\lambda(t-a)}M(t), the coefficient in the power inequality is bounded below by c e^{-\lambda(b-a)(p-1)}. Absolute continuity justifies integrating the negative-power derivative. Positivity and finiteness at b force the strict opposite of the displayed threshold, a contradiction.

For classical solutions of u_t-\Delta u=u^2 the same moment gives a lifespan, Kaplan's bound (Kaplan 1963). The moment \eta(t)=\int_\Omega w\,u(t) satisfies the Riccati inequality \eta'\ge\eta^2-\lambda\eta, and the solution of \eta'=\eta^2-\lambda\eta from \eta_0>\lambda blows up at \lambda^{-1}\log(\eta_0/(\eta_0-\lambda)).

Let \Omega\subset\mathbb R^n be nonempty, bounded and open. Let w\ge0 be C^2 in \Omega, continuous on \overline\Omega and zero on \partial\Omega, with -\Delta w=\lambda w in \Omega, \lambda>0 and \int_\Omega w=1. Let g\ge0 on \Omega with

\eta_0=\int_\Omega w\,g>\lambda.

Suppose u is C^2 in (0,T)\times\Omega, continuous on [0,T]\times\overline\Omega, solves u_t-\Delta u=u^2 in (0,T)\times\Omega, vanishes on (0,T)\times\partial\Omega and equals g at t=0. Then

T\le\frac1\lambda\log\frac{\eta_0}{\eta_0-\lambda}.

In particular there is no such solution for every T>0. No derivative of u or w on the boundary and no regularity of the boundary are used.

Proof for Theorem 6.156
uses 0

The minimum principle makes u nonnegative. Testing the equation against w, the diffusion term becomes -\lambda\eta, and Jensen's inequality for the probability weight w gives \int_\Omega w\,u^2\ge\eta^2, so \eta'\ge\eta^2-\lambda\eta. Since no boundary derivative of u is available, the formal proof tests against compactly supported convex truncations of w and absorbs their error into a slightly larger damping \lambda+\delta. For v=1/\eta the inequality reads v'\le\lambda v-1, and comparison with the solution of v'=\lambda v-1 keeps v positive only while 1-e^{-\lambda t}<\lambda/\eta_0. Letting \delta\to0 gives 1-e^{-\lambda T}\le\lambda/\eta_0, which is the bound.

For every p>1 and finite time T, define the spatially constant field

u(x,t)=\big((p-1)(T-t)\big)^{-\frac{1}{p-1}}, \qquad t<T.

This is the spatially homogeneous solution of the scalar equation u_t=u^p, viewed as a function on \mathbb R^n. It comes with a complete PDE and norm-divergence proof.

This whole-space example isolates the spatially homogeneous ODE blow-up mechanism. Its slices are nonzero constants, so it satisfies no homogeneous Dirichlet condition and, in positive dimension, does not lie in L^2(\mathbb R^n).

    def PDE.Solution.Singularity.FiniteTime.NonlinearHeat.constantBlowUp
  {n : ℕ} (p T : ℝ) (_x : ℝ^n) (t : ℝ) : ℝ

    The spatially constant blow-up candidate with exponent p and time T.

    The formula is defined for every t; it is a classical solution for p > 1 and t < T.

For this field the two halves of a blow-up result, the PDE and the divergence, are independent theorems sharing the hypotheses p>1 and t<T. The PDE half is elementary because the Laplacian of a spatially constant field vanishes, leaving only the ordinary differential equation u_t=u^p.

This makes the competition with smoothing precise. Diffusion acts on spatial variation, and this profile has none; the reaction still raises its height. For a positive scalar state, separation of variables gives

\frac{d}{dt}u^{1-p}=1-p, \qquad u(t)^{1-p}=u(t_0)^{1-p}-(p-1)(t-t_0).

The right-hand side reaches zero in finite time, forcing u to diverge. The solution stays smooth at every earlier time. Positive-time spatial smoothing therefore does not, by itself, bound amplitude or guarantee global existence.

The constant-profile solution theorem for the nonlinear heat equation states that on \mathbb R^n\times(-\infty,T), the field is a nonnegative classical solution of

u_t=\Delta u+u^p.

The equation field of the classical-solution proof is the constant-profile equation theorem, proved without the Type I profile theory. The formal theorem also checks joint spacetime C^1 regularity, C^2 regularity of every spatial slice, and positivity on the entire pre-singular cylinder.

    The positive real-power base gives joint spacetime C¹ regularity on the open domain. Every spatial slice is constant and hence globally C²; constantBlowUp_equation supplies the pointwise equation.

Proof for Theorem 6.158
uses 0

Let a=1/(p-1) and s=(p-1)(T-t)>0. The field is independent of x, so every spatial derivative and hence \Delta u vanishes. The real-power chain rule gives u_t=s^{-a-1} after the factor p-1 cancels a; since ap=a+1, this equals u^p. Positivity of s also gives positivity and the required smoothness on t<T.

Divergence is simpler still, since a constant slice has supremum equal to its common value. The explicit formula for S_u(t) is what makes the constant example a complete blow-up solution rather than a profile calculation.

S_u(t) =\operatorname{ofReal}\!\left( \big((p-1)(T-t)\big)^{-\frac{1}{p-1}} \right),

uses 0

The spatial supremum is at least the value at any fixed point and, because the field is constant, equals that value. As t\uparrow T, the positive base (p-1)(T-t) tends to zero. The exponent -1/(p-1) is negative, so the power tends to +\infty. Passing through ENNReal.ofReal preserves this divergence. The displayed supremum identity supplies finiteness at every preceding time.

Combining the two theorems gives an explicit classical solution whose spatial supremum norm diverges at the prescribed time.

Proof for Theorem 6.160
uses 0

Choose the explicitly defined constant field. The equation theorem supplies its nonnegative pointwise classical-solution structure on the full pre-singular cylinder, and the divergence theorem supplies spatial supremum-norm blow-up at T. Combining those two facts for the same witness proves the existential statement.

Separation of variables also identifies every solution of the scalar equation u'=u^p from a positive value, so the blow-up time of the constant field is the exact lifespan of the ODE.

Let p>1 and u_0>0, and set

T_p(u_0)=\frac{u_0^{1-p}}{p-1},\qquad u_*(t)=\big((p-1)(T_p(u_0)-t)\big)^{-\frac{1}{p-1}}.

uses 0

The derivative and the divergence of u_* are those of the constant field at any spatial point. For the converse, u stays at least u_0, since its right derivative u_0^p is positive wherever it equals u_0. Then u^{1-p} has right derivative 1-p on [0,T), so u(t)^{1-p}=u_0^{1-p}-(p-1)t. The left side is positive on [0,T], which is T<T_p(u_0), and solving for u gives u_*.

For a real exponent p and an open time set I, this structure records a nonnegative classical solution of

u_t=\Delta u+u^p

on \mathbb R^n\times I. Its regularity scope is joint spacetime C^1 for u together with C^2 regularity of each spatial slice. Time differentiability is derived from the joint C^1 field; joint C^{2,1} regularity is not required. The equation is imposed only at times in I, so a solution on t<T says nothing at T.

  {n : ℕ} (p : ℝ) (I : Set ℝ)
  (u : ℝ^n → ℝ → ℝ) : Prop

    A nonnegative pointwise classical solution of uₜ = Δu + uᵖ on an open time domain I, in the superlinear regime p > 1.

    The exponent condition excludes negative exponents, where Mathlib's convention 0 ^ p = 0 would let a zero value satisfy the equation spuriously. Spatial slices are defined on all of ℝ^n; only time is restricted. The regularity fields say that the spacetime function is jointly C¹ and that every admitted spatial slice is globally C². They do not require the spatial Hessian to depend continuously on time and therefore do not claim joint C^{2,1} regularity.

    The Fujita blow-up theorems use HeatEquation.Nonlinear.IsClassicalWholeSpacePowerSolution instead: a closed cylinder [0, T] × ℝⁿ with initial data and continuity up to t = 0.

    The singularity theory in this namespace concerns the superlinear regime.

    Joint spacetime C¹ regularity on ℝ^n × I.

    Spatial C² regularity of every admitted time slice.

    The pointwise nonlinear heat equation on the spacetime domain.

A profile must satisfy the stated regularity, sign and equation conditions. The Type I exponents make \Delta u, u_t, and u^p all scale by the same power of T-t.

For the Type I ansatz

u(x,t)=(T-t)^{-1/(p-1)} f\!\left(\frac{x-x_0}{\sqrt{T-t}}\right),

The reduced elliptic residual is

\Delta f-\frac12 y\cdot\nabla f-\frac{1}{p-1}f+f^p=0,

and the Type I profile equation says exactly that this residual vanishes pointwise. This is the standard Type I reduction used by Giga–Kohn, Comm. Pure Appl. Math. 38 (1985), DOI 10.1002/cpa.3160380304; the Lean statements are the exact substitution identities.

Proof for Theorem 6.164
uses 0

Write s=T-t, \alpha=1/(p-1), and y=s^{-1/2}(x-x_0). The backward similarity chain rules give u_t=s^{-\alpha-1}(\alpha f+\frac12y\cdot\nabla f) and \Delta u=s^{-\alpha-1}\Delta f, because two spatial scale factors produce s^{-1}. Nonnegativity permits u^p=s^{-\alpha p}f^p, and \alpha p=\alpha+1. Factoring s^{-\alpha-1} leaves the stated profile residual.

Since the prefactor (T-t)^{-(1/(p-1)+1)} is strictly positive for t<T, the residual identity upgrades at once to a profile equivalence.

Proof for Theorem 6.165
uses 0

The factorization writes the full residual as the profile residual multiplied by (T-t)^{-(1/(p-1)+1)}. For t<T, this prefactor is strictly positive and hence nonzero. Therefore the product vanishes exactly when the profile residual at the corresponding similarity point vanishes. Applying this pointwise to the Type I profile equation hypothesis proves the equation everywhere.

The pointwise equation is one field of the classical-solution record. The others, regularity and sign, are inherited from the profile because the amplitude and the similarity scale are smooth and positive before T. Assembling all of them needs the global hypotheses, nonnegativity everywhere and p>1, that the pointwise identity did not.

For a positive scale \lambda(t), the concentration ansatz is

u(x,t)=\lambda(t)^{-2/(p-1)} Q\!\left(\lambda(t)^{-1}(x-x_0)\right).

Its stationary elliptic residual is

\mathcal R_{\mathrm{stat}}[Q](y)=\Delta Q(y)+Q(y)^p,

and the stationary profile equation says exactly that this residual vanishes pointwise.

The exponent is invariant under the nonlinear-heat equation scaling. Whether that scaling is critical for a particular Sobolev or Lebesgue norm also depends on the dimension and exponent, hence the name "scaling-invariant" rather than "critical".

Type II blow-up constructions with this leading profile, such as the modulation analyses of Schweyer (arXiv:1201.2907v2) and of Collot (2017), add correction terms and prove the asymptotic law of the scale. The residual and rigidity identities here concern the pure profile.

Suppose p\ne1, Q is C^2 and nonnegative at y=\lambda(t)^{-1}(x-x_0), and the scale is positive and differentiable at t. Write

Thus the formal identity separates the stationary elliptic error from the modulation defect.

    Exact criterion for the pure concentration ansatz to solve the equation at one point.

    For a stationary elliptic profile and a positive scale, the residual can vanish only because the scale is instantaneously stationary or because the profile is annihilated by the scaling generator at the corresponding similarity coordinate.

Proof for Theorem 6.170
uses 1

Positivity of \lambda(t) makes the common power of \lambda(t) nonzero. The residual therefore vanishes exactly when \lambda(t)\lambda'(t)\Lambda Q(y)=0. Removing the second nonzero scale factor and splitting the remaining product yields the two alternatives.

At the center x=x_0 the similarity coordinate is y=0, the Euler term of \Lambda Q disappears, and \Lambda Q(0)=\frac{2}{p-1}Q(0). When Q(0)>0 the second branch of the criterion is unavailable and the first is forced; positivity at the origin also supplies the sign hypothesis the criterion needs at that one coordinate.

    If a stationary profile is positive at the origin and its pure concentration ansatz solves the equation at the center, then the scale is instantaneously stationary.

Proof for Theorem 6.171
uses 1

At x=x_0 the similarity variable is zero, so \Lambda Q(0)=\frac{2}{p-1}Q(0). This quantity is nonzero because p\ne1 and Q(0)>0; hence the scaling-generator branch of the pointwise criterion is impossible, and \lambda'(t)=0.

Center rigidity is infinitesimal: it fixes \lambda' at one time. On an open connected time set where the center equation holds throughout, the vanishing derivative integrates to a constant scale, so a pure profile with positive center admits no nontrivial modulation law at all.

Proof for Theorem 6.172
uses 1

Apply center rigidity at every point of I to obtain \lambda'=0 throughout the interval. Since an open connected subset of \mathbb R is an interval, the mean-value theorem applied between any two of its points shows that their scale values agree.

The rigidity statements look at one spatial point, the center. Requiring instead that the residual vanish at every spatial point at a fixed time gives a global form of the pointwise criterion, because inverse dilation reaches every similarity coordinate.

Proof for Theorem 6.173
uses 1

If \lambda'(t)=0, the pointwise criterion settles every spatial point. Otherwise it forces \Lambda Q to vanish at every similarity coordinate. Every y\in\mathbb R^n occurs by choosing x=x_0+\lambda(t)y, because the positive scale is invertible. Conversely, either global alternative implies the pointwise disjunction for each x.

None of the residual statements says anything about size. The divergence theorem is independent of all of them: it concerns the field defined by the formula and holds whether or not the field solves the equation.

Proof for Theorem 6.174
uses 0

Choose y_0 with Q(y_0)\ne0 and sample the field at x(t)=x_0+\lambda(t)y_0. There the profile argument is exactly y_0, so the absolute value is \lambda(t)^{-2/(p-1)}|Q(y_0)|. Since p>1 and \lambda(t)\to0^+, this quantity tends to +\infty and is bounded above by the spatial supremum. If |Q(y)|\le C everywhere, the same formula bounds the whole slice by the finite number \lambda(t)^{-2/(p-1)}C whenever \lambda(t)>0. Positivity holds eventually by the scale-limit hypothesis.

6.7.1.7. Parabolic Keller–Segel Similarity Reduction🔗

Similarity variables separate the universal singular scale from the shape of a possible blow-up profile. For Keller–Segel, the parabolic scale balances diffusion, chemotactic drift, and the time derivative: space contracts like (T-t)^{1/2} while density grows like (T-t)^{-1}. Substitution reduces the physical PDE to a stationary pair of profile residuals.

uses 0used by 1✓L∃∀N

On an open time set I, classical parabolic–elliptic Keller–Segel solutions use the sign convention

u_t=\operatorname{div}(\nabla u-u\nabla\Phi),\qquad -\Delta\Phi=u.

The density is nonnegative and jointly C^1 in spacetime, the potential is jointly continuous, and both have C^2 spatial slices; joint C^{2,1} regularity is not required. The elliptic equation alone determines \Phi only up to a harmonic component, and the definition imposes neither a Newtonian-potential normalization nor decay at spatial infinity.

    The density equation in conservative form.

    potential_equation : ∀ (x : ℝ^d), ∀ t ∈ I, -PDE.laplacian (fun y ↦ Φ y t) x = u x t

    The elliptic equation for the chemoattractant potential.

The parabolic ansatz has to be matched to these equations one by one. The density carries the amplitude (T-t)^{-1} and the potential carries none, because two spatial derivatives of a function of y=(T-t)^{-1/2}(x-x_0) already produce the factor (T-t)^{-1} that -\Delta\Phi=u demands.

For t<T, write

y=(T-t)^{-1/2}(x-x_0),\qquad u_Q(x,t)=(T-t)^{-1}Q(y),\qquad \Phi_\Psi(x,t)=\Psi(y).

The reduced residuals are

\mathcal R_\Phi[Q,\Psi]=-\Delta\Psi-Q,\qquad \mathcal R_Q[Q,\Psi] =\operatorname{div}(\nabla Q-Q\nabla\Psi) -Q-\frac12 y\mathbin{\cdot}\nabla Q.

The two equations are represented by separate residual functions, defined in every finite dimension without regularity or sign assumptions.

Proof for Theorem 6.177
uses 0

The Laplacian of the scaled potential contributes the square of the spatial dilation factor. Before T, the identity ((T-t)^{-1/2})^2=(T-t)^{-1} makes this factor equal to the density amplitude. Expanding the potential residual and collecting the common factor gives the stated profile residual.

The density residual is assembled from two separate scaling computations, the time derivative and the flux divergence, which must produce the same power of T-t for the reduction to close. The time derivative is where the Euler term \frac12 y\cdot\nabla Q originates.

Proof for Theorem 6.178
uses 0

Apply the general differentiation formula for a backward self-similar ansatz with amplitude exponent 1 and spatial exponent 1/2. The derivative of the amplitude gives Q(y), while differentiation of the moving coordinate gives \frac12 y\mathbin{\cdot}\nabla Q(y). Both terms carry the common factor (T-t)^{-2}.

The flux \nabla u-u\nabla\Phi is where the scaling of \Phi_\Psi matters: with no amplitude on the potential, u\nabla\Phi carries the same factors as \nabla u, so diffusion and drift scale together, and one more divergence gives the same (T-t)^{-2} as the time derivative.

Proof for Theorem 6.179
uses 0

The density gradient scales by (T-t)^{-1}(T-t)^{-1/2}, and the potential gradient by (T-t)^{-1/2}. Hence both terms in the flux share the first factor. Taking one more divergence contributes another (T-t)^{-1/2}. The identity ((T-t)^{-1/2})^2=(T-t)^{-1} then combines the factors into (T-t)^{-2}.

With both pieces carrying (T-t)^{-2}, their difference is the density residual identity.

At every fixed time t<T, the similarity substitution loses no spatial information. Positivity of the scale and inverse dilation give the two exact equivalences

\begin{aligned} \mathcal R_\Phi[u_Q,\Phi_\Psi](\mathbin{\cdot},t)=0 &\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \mathcal R_\Phi[Q,\Psi]=0,\\ \mathcal R_u[u_Q,\Phi_\Psi](\mathbin{\cdot},t)=0 &\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \mathcal R_Q[Q,\Psi]=0. \end{aligned}

Each physical equation is also equivalent pointwise to its reduced equation at the corresponding similarity coordinate. The elliptic direction requires \Psi\in C^2; the density direction requires Q,\Psi\in C^2.

Proof for Theorem 6.181
uses 0

The forward direction of each equivalence evaluates the physical residual at x=x_0+s^{-1}y, where s=(T-t)^{-1/2}. The scale is positive, and the centered dilation sends this x back to y. The residual factorization then has a nonzero scalar factor, so the profile residual must vanish. The reverse direction substitutes the vanishing profile residual directly into the same factorization.

The equivalences supply the two equations of a classical solution; the solution theorem adds regularity and the sign of the density.

Proof for Theorem 6.182
uses 0

Generic regularity lemmas for scaled profiles give joint C^1 regularity of the density, joint continuity of the potential, and C^2 regularity of every spatial slice. Positivity of the amplitude transfers Q\geq0 to the physical density. Finally, the two residual factorizations turn the assumed profile equations into the density and potential equations at every t<T.

The solution theorem is silent about size and the blow-up theorem is silent about the equations. A Keller–Segel blow-up solution arises when one profile pair meets the hypotheses of both theorems.

Proof for Theorem 6.183
uses 0

Choose a physical sample whose similarity coordinate is the point where Q is nonzero. Along this sample the profile value is fixed, while the amplitude (T-t)^{-1} tends to +\infty. The general backward self-similar blow-up theorem transfers this sampled divergence to the extended spatial supremum. A global bound |Q(y)|\le C bounds each slice by the finite value (T-t)^{-1}C for t<T.

6.7.1.8. Keller–Segel Virial Horizon🔗

6.7.1.8.1. Two-dimensional Keller–Segel virial horizon🔗

The virial mechanism turns a question about how long a PDE solution lives into a contradiction between two numbers. In the supercritical two-dimensional regime, the normalized Keller–Segel second moment decreases at a constant rate. A nonnegative density cannot have a negative second moment, so a classical solution satisfying the virial hypotheses cannot survive past the moment when that affine quantity hits zero.

uses 0used by 1✓L∃∀N

For mass M>8\pi, define

\gamma(M)=\frac{M^2}{2\pi}-4M>0, \qquad T_{\mathrm{vir}}=\frac{I(0)}{\gamma(M)}.

For the whole-space system with sensitivity one and the normalized Newtonian potential, the classical second-moment identity is I'(t)=-\gamma(M) (Blanchet–Dolbeault–Perthame, Electron. J. Differential Equations 2006(44), Theorem 1.1 and equation (2.3)).

The pointwise Keller–Segel solution predicate does not fix this normalization: adding a harmonic function to \Phi preserves -\Delta\Phi=u but can change the drift. A PDE derivation of the sharp virial law therefore also needs the Newtonian normalization or equivalent decay, finite moments, mass conservation, differentiation under the integral, and justified integration by parts. The theorems take the resulting scalar derivative identity as a hypothesis.

Proof for Theorem 6.185
uses 0

Rewrite the assumed derivative as the constant -\gamma(M). The lower and upper mean-value inequalities on the convex interval [0,T] then bound I(t)-I(0) from both sides by -\gamma(M)t. The two bounds coincide, which gives the affine identity.

Supercritical mass enters at this point, through \gamma(M)>0: the affine function is then strictly decreasing and crosses zero at T_{\mathrm{vir}}.

Suppose T\geq0, the second moment is continuous on [0,T], differentiable on (0,T), and satisfies the virial identity there. If M>8\pi and the second moment is nonnegative at T, then

T\le T_{\mathrm{vir}}.

The endpoint T is any time up to which the hypotheses hold. Jäger–Luckhaus, Trans. Amer. Math. Soc. 329 (1992), DOI 10.1090/S0002-9947-1992-1046835-6, is the historical background for radial explosion arguments; the whole-space identity is the one of Blanchet–Dolbeault–Perthame.

Proof for Theorem 6.186
uses 0

Supercritical mass makes \gamma(M) positive. If the endpoint lay strictly beyond I(0)/\gamma(M), the affine formula at T would give I(T)=I(0)-\gamma(M)T<0. This contradicts the assumed nonnegativity of the endpoint moment.

The scalar theorem never mentions a density. The density-level version derives the one hypothesis the scalar statement cannot see, nonnegativity of I_u(T), from pointwise nonnegativity of the slice at T.

For a density u : \mathbb R^2\to\mathbb R\to\mathbb R, define its mass and second moment directly by

M_u(t)=\int_{\mathbb R^2}u(x,t)\,dx, \qquad I_u(t)=\int_{\mathbb R^2}|x|^2u(x,t)\,dx.

These are totalized Bochner integrals. The theorem assumes T\geq0 and a finite quadratic moment on every slice in [0,T]; the nonzero conserved mass certifies integrability of the density slices. If u(\cdot,T) is pointwise nonnegative, M_u(t)=M>8\pi, and I_u has the required continuity, differentiability, and virial identity, then

T\le \frac{I_u(0)}{M^2/(2\pi)-4M}.

Mass conservation and the differentiated virial law are hypotheses.

6.7.1.9. Abnormal Three-Dimensional Keller–Segel Scaling🔗

An abnormal similarity scale is useful only if one distinguishes an asymptotic profile equation from the exact physical PDE. In the three-dimensional construction studied here, diffusion carries a coefficient that vanishes in rescaled variables. The leading aggregation profile can therefore describe the asymptotic balance without itself being an exact solution, and the analytic construction adds perturbative correction terms.

For modes j\ge4, the Liu–Wang–Zhou abnormal scaling uses

\beta_j=\frac13+\frac{1}{2j}, \qquad \delta_j=1-2\beta_j=\frac13-\frac1j>0.

The exponent lies strictly between 1/3 and the parabolic value 1/2. Consequently diffusion enters the rescaled density equation with the lower-order coefficient (T-t)^{\delta_j}.

The scaling follows Liu et al. (2025), Theorem 1.1 and equations (1.8), (1.12), and (1.13), with \mu=0. The Lean development treats the leading ansatz, the exponent arithmetic, and the residual identities.

    For every abnormal mode j ≥ 4, the coefficient of the diffusion perturbation tends to zero at the proposed singular time.

    This is the analytic content of βⱼ < 1/2: diffusion is lower order than aggregation after rescaling, although it does not vanish identically before the singular time.

Proof for Theorem 6.189
uses 0

The mode assumption gives \delta_j=\frac13-\frac1j>0. The base T-t tends to zero as t\uparrow T, and continuity of r\mapsto r^{\delta_j} at zero for a positive exponent sends this limit to zero.

The density amplitude is (T-t)^{-1}, the same as in the parabolic scaling, so the abnormal density ansatz diverges for the same reason. The mode restriction plays no role here; it matters only for the exponent estimates.

A bounded density profile that is nonzero at one point makes the abnormal density ansatz blow up in spatial supremum norm at T: its slices are finite and their supremum diverges because the amplitude is (T-t)^{-1}. Without boundedness, the extended supremum still diverges.

    A bounded abnormal density profile with one nonzero value makes its ansatz blow up in spatial supremum norm at the proposed singular time.

    Only the scaling of the density ansatz is used; the profile need not solve the profile equations.

Proof for Theorem 6.190
uses 0

Apply the general backward self-similar blow-up theorem with amplitude exponent 1 and spatial exponent \beta_j. A moving spatial sample keeps the similarity coordinate at a point where Q is nonzero, so its norm is a fixed positive constant times (T-t)^{-1}. The global profile bound also bounds each spatial slice by a finite multiple of this amplitude for t<T.

Divergence of the formula says nothing about whether it solves Keller–Segel, and in general it does not. The residual identity makes this quantitative: under the diffusion-free aggregation equation, the density residual is the diffusion term that equation omits.

Suppose Q,\Phi\in C^2, t<T, and the pair satisfies the diffusion-free aggregation profile equation at the displayed similarity coordinate. Exact substitution into the density equation leaves

\mathcal R_u(x,t) =(T-t)^{-2}(T-t)^{\delta_j} \Delta Q\!\left((T-t)^{-\beta_j}(x-x_0)\right).

The identity separates the singular physical prefactor from the lower-order profile error.

    A diffusion-free abnormal profile leaves exactly the lower-order diffusion residual.

Proof for Theorem 6.191
uses 0

The exact substitution theorem factors the physical residual as -(T-t)^{-2} times the abnormal profile residual. Under the diffusion-free aggregation equation, every term in that profile residual cancels except -(T-t)^{\delta_j}\Delta Q. Multiplying the two negative factors gives the displayed diffusion error.

The two factors of the diffusion error pull in opposite directions, and the exponent arithmetic decides which wins: -2+\delta_j=-(1+2\beta_j)<0.

Assume j\ge4, the profiles are C^2, the diffusion-free aggregation profile equation holds everywhere, and \Delta Q(0)\ne0. At the similarity center, the exact residual identity reduces to

\left|\mathcal R_u(x_0,t)\right| = (T-t)^{-(1+2\beta_j)}|\Delta Q(0)|.

Since 1+2\beta_j>0, this physical residual tends to +\infty as t\uparrow T, while the rescaled diffusion coefficient tends to zero.

    The physical density residual of an uncorrected abnormal profile diverges at the similarity center whenever the profile is nonharmonic there.

    At x = center, the similarity coordinate is 0, so the diffusion-free profile equation cancels the aggregation terms. Exact substitution leaves (T - t)⁻² (T - t)^(1 - 2βⱼ) ΔQ(0) = (T - t)^(-(1 + 2βⱼ)) ΔQ(0). For j ≥ 4, the exponent 1 + 2βⱼ is positive; thus ΔQ(0) ≠ 0 forces the norm of the physical residual to tend to +∞, even though the rescaled diffusion coefficient tends to zero.

Proof for Theorem 6.192
uses 0

At x=x_0, the centered dilation is zero. Combine (T-t)^{-2} with (T-t)^{1-2\beta_j} to obtain (T-t)^{-(1+2\beta_j)}. The mode bound implies 1+2\beta_j>0, so this power tends to +\infty; multiplication by the positive constant |\Delta Q(0)| preserves the limit.

Divergence at the center is a statement about one point and one limit. The exact criterion is a statement at every fixed pre-singular time.

used by 0✓L∃∀N

Suppose Q,\Phi\in C^2 and the diffusion-free aggregation profile equation holds at every profile point. At any fixed t<T, the uncorrected abnormal ansatz has zero density residual at every spatial point if and only if

\Delta Q(y)=0\qquad\text{for every }y\in\mathbb R^3.

This is an exact no-go theorem for nonharmonic leading profiles. It concerns the density equation; the elliptic potential equation is a separate condition.

    Global obstruction for the uncorrected abnormal density ansatz at one pre-singular time.

    The leading aggregation profile equation omits diffusion. Exact substitution restores the term (T - t)^(1 - 2βⱼ) ΔQ, whose coefficient is nonzero for every t < T; inverse dilation shows that the physical residual samples every profile coordinate. Hence the exact density residual vanishes everywhere exactly when Q is harmonic everywhere. This concerns only the density residual of the uncorrected ansatz.

Proof for Theorem 6.193
uses 0

At a fixed pre-singular time, positivity of the physical prefactor and inverse dilation reduce global vanishing of the physical residual to global vanishing of the profile residual. The aggregation equation rewrites that profile residual as a nonzero positive power of T-t times -\Delta Q(y). It therefore vanishes at every profile point exactly when \Delta Q does.
